resources.string: How skin holds on to water
An educational view of epidermal renewal and the surface barrier. Water paths are qualitative, not measured water loss.
New cells start at the base
Basal cells replenish the epidermis. Older keratinocytes are displaced toward the surface.
Cells flatten on the way up
As keratinocytes differentiate toward the surface, they flatten. The outermost corneocytes no longer have nuclei.
Granular cells release lipids outside the cell. The lipids organize into layers around flattened corneocytes.
An intact barrier slows water loss
Some water still diffuses outward. Disrupting the layers between cells makes water loss easier.
The surface sheds and is renewed
Outer corneocytes shed while newly differentiated cells replace them from below. The barrier continually renews.
How sperm form, mature and travel
An educational view of the male reproductive tract and cell maturation. Motion and timings are not individual measurements.
Germ cells develop beside Sertoli cells. After meiosis and changes in shape, sperm are released from the wall into the lumen.
Fluid in the ducts helps carry sperm through the rete testis and efferent ducts into the head of the epididymis.
During passage through the coiled epididymal duct, sperm membranes change and the capacity for forward movement develops.
Temporary storage in the epididymal tail
Mature sperm can be stored in the tail of the epididymis. The ability to swim does not mean sperm propel themselves through the entire tract.
During ejaculation, contractions of smooth muscle in the vas deferens propel duct fluid and sperm.
How an oocyte is released and enters the tube
An educational view of ovulation and tubal transport, not a tool for predicting ovulation or pregnancy.
A follicle in the ovary grows. The oocyte remains inside, surrounded by supporting cumulus cells.
At ovulation, the follicle opens near the surface of the ovary and releases the oocyte with the surrounding cumulus cells.
The fimbriae pick up the oocyte
The ovary is not directly connected to the tube opening. Nearby fimbriae and their cilia help guide the oocyte into the opening.
Cilia beat and the wall assists
Cilia beat directionally and smooth muscle in the wall contracts. Both contribute to tubal transport.
The oocyte reaches the wider ampulla, the usual site of fertilization. Ovulation is not fertilization or implantation.
